methodology_content:
Data Collection Process

All incident data is automatically collected from Hebrew Wikipedia's comprehensive documentation of the Gilad Shalit prisoner exchange deal. Wikipedia footnotes are used as primary sources for verification.

Source Verification Methodology

Every incident must meet the following criteria:

  • Minimum 1 source: Each incident is verified by at least one reliable source from Wikipedia footnotes
  • Automatic extraction: Sources are automatically extracted from Wikipedia references
  • Accessibility: All source URLs are checked for accessibility and validity
  • No social media: Social media posts and forums are strictly excluded from sources

Approved Publishers

Israeli News: Ynet, Haaretz, Times of Israel, Jerusalem Post, i24NEWS, Israel Hayom, Maariv

American News: New York Times, Washington Post, CNN, Reuters, AP News, NBC News, Wall Street Journal

Government & Reference: Israeli Government websites, Wikipedia

Blocked Sources

The following sources are strictly prohibited:

  • Social media platforms: Facebook, Twitter/X, Instagram, TikTok, Telegram
  • Forums: Reddit
  • Personal blogs and unverified websites

Data Quality Standards

All incidents are automatically extracted and verified:

  • Sources from Wikipedia footnotes
  • Clear documentation from reliable publishers
  • Automatic validation of source accessibility
  • Bilingual information (English and Hebrew)

Updates and Corrections

This dataset is regularly reviewed and updated. If you notice any errors or have additional verified information, please contact us with credible sources.

about_content:
The issue of releasing terrorists stirs deep and ongoing controversy in Israeli public discourse, especially when it arises in the context of prisoner exchange deals or attempts to return hostages and missing soldiers.

Naturally, the main discourse regarding the "price" that the State of Israel pays revolves around the "blood on the hands" of the released terrorists—namely, how many Israelis they murdered in the past (for example, The Real Price Project).

The less discussed issue is the future price that the State of Israel must pay—that is, the number of Israelis who are murdered as a result of terrorist release deals. For anyone who has worked in a security role dealing with terrorism and is familiar with the history of similar deals, it is crystal clear that Israelis will almost certainly be murdered as a result of any future deal in which a large number of terrorists are released.

The idea to create a system for making information about the future price of terrorist release deals more accessible came to me after watching an (excellent) interview by Roni Kuban with former Shin Bet Director Yoram Cohen. During the interview, the former Shin Bet Director was asked if he felt any guilt about the release of Yahya Sinwar (who planned and executed the largest terrorist attack in the history of the State of Israel) as part of the Shalit deal. The former Shin Bet Director replied that he feels no regret because even today he supports such deals, although "it is clear to him that the deals will cause the murder of Israelis." Roni Kuban's response was one of total shock ("Wow" in his words). This simple scene made me realize that this very basic knowledge—that releasing terrorists certainly causes future murders—is not sufficiently known in the Israeli public discourse.

Within this system, I have attempted to make accessible, based only on reliable journalistic reports, all documented cases of terrorists who murdered Israelis after being released in prisoner exchange deals. Unfortunately, the Ministry of Defense does not publish this data, so the vast majority of information about murder victims is available to us mainly from the last decade—namely, the Gilad Shalit exchange deal.

This system went live only after the release of all hostages in the recent deal. Now, when there is no Israeli hostage held by the enemy, it is time to discuss these issues.

If you notice any inaccuracies or missing information in the data, please don't hesitate to reach out to us at: the.unspoken.price.tag@gmail.com
